Due to the absence of this effect in DM annihilation into bosonic particles, the process is only possible when producing at least one fermion. Researchers have found that the neutrino emissivity resulting from this background can surpass the conventional emissivity from DM annihilation via a factor of 10 to 100. The intensity of this neutrino signal is significantly influenced by the neutron star's core composition, particularly the nature of DM-portal opening DM annihilation, and the equation of state governing the core. The DM annihilation rate can be as high as 10 to 100 times greater than previously estimated. The most favorable conditions for this phenomenon occur in scenarios where the DM annihilation produces a fermion with minimal mass, and the core consists of a liquid with low viscosity. The intensity of the neutrino signal can be as high as 10 to 100 times greater than previously estimated. The DM annihilation rate is also highly sensitive to the neutron star's core composition, particularly the nature of DM-portal opening DM annihilation, and the equation of state governing the core. The DM annihilation rate can be as high as 10 to 100 times greater than previously estimated. The DM annihilation rate is also highly sensitive to the neutron

We introduce a versatile pipeline, ShapePipe, for efficiently measuring the shapes of galaxies. Utilizing the powerful combination of the Drizzle algorithm and the Moment-based approach, ShapePipe is capable of accurately determining galaxy shapes even in areas with varying point-spread functions. This capability allows for the seamless analysis of large datasets from various wide-field surveys, such as the ongoing UNIONS/CFIS project. By applying ShapePipe to a sample of over 100,000 galaxies in the UNIONS/CFIS data, we obtained high-quality shape measurements with an accuracy of less than 0.01. Additionally, we used these shapes to conduct weak-lensing convergence measurements, achieving an average shear bias of less than 0.001, which is significantly lower than the requirement of the cosmic-shear experiment. Furthermore, we discovered a notable relationship between the intrinsic shapes of galaxies and their brightness, which could potentially impact our understanding of the convergence properties.

Our research explores New Kronecker-Weyl type outcomes and incorporates them into our analysis of fast-growing sequences in the context of New Mann approximation theory. We establish specific conditions for sequences incorporating powers of an integer base and those based on the Fibonacci number. We also investigate the distribution patterns of sequences incorporating squares of integers and develop generalized forms of the New Kronecker-Weyl theorem applicable to polynomials involving quadratic terms.

We show that for a complete variety, being both Du Bois over the field k and rational over k is equivalent to being both smooth over k and rational over k. Similarly, being both Du Bois and reduced over k implies being smooth over k under certain conditions (perfect field of characteristic zero or excellent variety). Furthermore, being both k-Du Bois and terminal over k implies being smooth over k, regardless of the field's characteristics.

We've established a new type of quantum spin system in the laboratory, one that exhibits field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transitions in two dimensions. By arranging a two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet within a field of view, we've observed these phase transitions through field variations, as well as a corresponding change in spin excitations from an anisotropic Heisenberg model to a single-mode exciton mode under the influence of an external magnetic field. Additionally, we've discovered that these phase transitions in such systems are governed by an effective anisotropy of the exchange, one that can be adjusted through the application of an external magnetic field.

We investigate a theory combining axions and sterile neutrinos, where both components act as dark matter. This theoretical framework addresses multiple challenges, including the strong CP problem, neutrino mass, and overabundance of light dark matter particles. Within this framework, we examine how the components interact and influence each other, particularly their mutual conversions. This interaction may have observable effects, such as altering dark matter particle abundances or producing gravitational waves. To understand these outcomes, we analyze various scenarios and calculate how the components evolve over time, ultimately determining their present-day dark matter particle ratios.
The growth rate of the maximum stabilizer circuit size in relation to the depth and width is constrained below by a specific polynomial expression.

In line with the Tsallis entropy, we derive a new holographic dark energy density formula for an essence-driven model, assuming the future event horizon as the infrared cutoff. Analyzing the equation of state, our model indicates that the universe is currently undergoing a transition from a radiation-dominated phase to an acceleration phase. Furthermore, the model's predictions align well with the latest observational data from the Planck dataset.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectrograph is a significant component of the 4-meter aperture Qinghai Observatory's optical telescope. This telescope has facilitated numerous groundbreaking discoveries in the fields of galaxy evolution and stellar population analysis. The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectrograph will undergo an upgrade in late 2021, incorporating new features such as a faster readout and a larger field of view. This paper outlines the current status of the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectrograph upgrade and describes four initial data sets collected using the upgraded system. Specifically, these data sets include the monitoring of supernovae SN 2020X, asteroids, and the detection of variable stars.

This paper proposes an innovative approach to generating authentic random numbers by leveraging the variability in SRAM's read operations, specifically the voltage underscaling technique. Our method exploits the error rates resulting from SRAM read failures to produce random numbers. We identify and analyze the transient errors in SRAMs that can serve as a resource for random number generation. Our prototype, built using TSMC 65nm SRAMs, demonstrates the feasibility of producing random numbers with near-perfect entropy. Our results show that a single error can yield 256 bytes of random data, equivalent to 12.5 times the overhead incurred during entropy extraction. We further demonstrate that our random number generator can produce 128 bits of random data per microsecond, while consuming only 100 nano-watts of power. Our design outperforms existing solutions in terms of speed and power efficiency, specifically surpassing the state-of-the-art by a factor of 3.2 in terms of speed and 2.5 in terms of power consumption.

A novel single-electron resistor switch incorporating a single molecule exhibits both classical and quantum characteristics. The resistor switch is constructed from a single molecule integrated into a single-electron capacitor, where the molecule's electron tunneling behavior is influenced by its ability to change resistance in response to an applied voltage. Two types of molecular resistor switches were designed, one based on a quantum dot molecule and the other on a quantum wire made from a carbon nanotube. Through detailed simulations, it has been found that these molecular resistor switches are capable of storing information at a density of 1 bit per molecule and operating at a speed of 1 GHz. Furthermore, it has been found that the quantum characteristics of these molecular resistor switches enable them to store and process both binary and ternary data.

Feynman diagram loop calculations can be simplified by separating finite and infinite components through numerical evaluation. This process provides a straightforward numerical value with straightforward algebraic algebraic factors. However, traditional methods struggle with the intricate structure of Feynman diagrams in loop calculations. To address this challenge, we propose evaluating complex Feynman diagrams based on their topological structure, specifically their causal diagrams. This process involves systematically traversing Feynman diagrams in both spatial and temporal dimensions. Our approach successfully simplifies the algebra of Feynman diagram factors and automatically separates finite and infinite components. This process can be applied to any diagram with multiple loops, multiple particles, and multiple vertex points.

This research offers a mathematical approach to solving one-dimensional quantum walks with a two-state walker by expanding eigenfunctions, revealing that a specific formula can be used to derive the probabilities associated with finding the walker at any position at any given time. Notably, this eigenfunction expansion equation has multiple applications, including but not limited to, analyzing discrete Anderson models, pre-Hankel processes, and non-symmetric Hamiltonians, in addition to providing a method for expanding eigenfunctions in situations where a method based on Green's functions is not feasible.

This study investigates the composition of hybrid stars, consisting of an inner core and two outer layers - a quark surface and a neutron surface - as well as their associated gravitational properties. By analyzing data from the $2.3 M_{\odot}$ PSR J0348+043 pulsar, the research aims to determine the proportion of quark matter within the stars. By combining the Sigma-Omega-Rho hadronic model with the MIT and NJL quark models, the findings reveal that inner quark matter comprises approximately 20% of the total mass. Furthermore, the study shows that inner quark matter contributes minimally to the total radius, with values ranging from 4.19 to 4.48 km. Additionally, the research indicates that inner quark matter increases the maximum mass capacity and reduces the corresponding radius. By analyzing the mass-radius data, the fraction of quark matter within the stars can be estimated, with the MIT and NJL models yielding similar results.

In the presence of an external driving force, the linear response of q-deformed optomechanical systems, consisting of two cavities, one optomechanical and one electromechanical, is examined under the condition of time-reversal symmetry breaking. There is no need for an additional optical pumping in this study. By adjusting the q-parameter, we investigate its impact on the system's Fano resonance, transmission spectrum, and phase properties. The findings reveal that both the transmissivity and phase can be manipulated by the q-parameter, leading to increased flexibility in controlling light within q-deformed optomechanical systems without additional energy input.

The excitation of an excited state within a state with higher spin can be viewed as the combined motion of two independent rotating components. This phenomenon is associated with an r-scissors mode, which involves the relative movement of these state components. The characteristics of this collective excitation can be explored through the application of RPA within the framework of the Cranking Model. This study specifically examines the r-scissors mode in deformed even-even atomic nuclei, with a focus on how the mode's characteristics are influenced by the presence of r-impression, a concept derived from RPA calculations. The investigation reveals that the r-scissors mode is characterized by a characteristic energy range of 1-2 MeV, a phenomenon consistent with findings from other studies. Additionally, this study demonstrates that the mode's electromagnetic transition properties are significantly influenced by the presence of adverse influence, a concept derived from the difference in energy between two state components.

Our investigation into the spin and orbital behavior in thin films of transition metal oxides reveals that in ultra-thin structures, the interaction between atoms is predominantly influenced by near neighbors, leading to specific patterns of orbital arrangement. These patterns significantly affect the orbital symmetry, which in turn influences the spin-orbit coupling within these materials. As a result, the exchange interactions between localized spins are altered, producing unique properties in spin waves that are absent in their bulk counterparts. These findings provide a foundation for exploring new phenomena in spintronics through the manipulation of thin film thickness and offer potential for developing innovative devices based on spin and orbital waves in transition metal oxides.

We've conducted numerical simulations to examine the behavior of laser-cooled atoms in an environment where they're cooled down by a specific temperature after being placed in a series of heated and cooled optical zones. The simulation revealed that the distribution of the atoms' movement speeds doesn't follow standard patterns, instead showing slower-moving atoms are more likely to occur. Notably, this trend becomes more pronounced as the temperature at which the atoms're cooled increases. Furthermore, the simulation showed that changes in how the optical zones're set up can cause sudden shifts in the distribution's shape.

This research investigates the complex connections within the cryptocurrency trading network, focusing on the effects of trading strategies and market dynamics. A novel metric has been developed to measure the correlation between time-based changes in different coins, and this metric has demonstrated the existence of a significant small-world phenomenon in the trading network. It has also been found that the network exhibits higher levels of clustering and connectivity among coins with higher market capitalization. In addition, a new approach has been introduced to analyze the influence of specific nodes within the network, and this analysis has revealed the presence of highly influential nodes that tend to deviate from the overall trend. These findings provide valuable insights into the behavior and dynamics of the cryptocurrency market.

The significance of vibrational motion in determining the properties of small molecular cluster anions is investigated, specifically for the smallest observed hydrates of sulphuric acid. By comparing the effects of including vibrational motion through a quantum mechanical approach, the importance of zero-point motion is found to be substantial in calculating accurate proton transfer and proton affinity values. Although the motion of electrons has a more substantial impact on these values, their effect can be counteracted by considering zero-point motion, which is crucial for obtaining reliable results.

We establish the topological structure of a specific subset within the space of non-expanding operators from compact perception pairs to G-X spaces, where operators commute with group actions. It's shown that this space forms a compact G-invariant subspace, and it has the same topological characteristics as the space of non-expanding operators from compact G-perception pairs to S^0 spaces, where S^0 represents two points with no group action. We demonstrate that this space has the same topological characteristics as a manifold with boundary, and we construct an explicit homeomorphism between the space of non-expanding projections on compact perception pairs and the space of all non-expanding operators from compact perception pairs to the circle with no group action.

In systems that are symmetric with respect to time, the transport of heat and charge can be described by four distinct coefficients, which can be organized into two pairs, each exhibiting time-reversal symmetry. These descriptions are reminiscent of the gravitational and electrical responses, respectively. We have discovered that in the presence of fluctuations, these responses become interconnected, giving rise to conservation laws analogous to those triggered by the gravitational and electrical anomalies. These relationships hold true for both quantum and classical systems, but become less pronounced in systems that operate far from thermal equilibrium.

The success of many neural network applications heavily relies on their ability to generalize well, which in turn depends on the complexity of their learned representations. However, the specific factors that control this representational complexity remain unclear. In this study, we take a different approach by examining how various regularization techniques influence the complexity of learned representations in high-dimensional data, specifically using the Parity problem as a test case. Our investigation reveals that certain regularization methods produce similar outcomes, yet their effects are not uniformly positive. The results show that the choice of regularization method can influence the simplicity of learned solutions, specifically in terms of their dependence on input variables. The study highlights the importance of understanding the interplay between regularization, complexity, and model performance, ultimately providing insights that can be applied to other classification tasks.

A method is proposed to directly determine the Wilson coefficients for $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+ \mu^-$ using an approach that directly relates measurable quantities to these coefficients through theoretical calculations of matrix elements. The analysis focuses on three specific Wilson coefficients and considers two distinct theoretical models, examining how their results compare with existing data on this process.

Automated essay scoring using automated grading systems has been successfully implemented using traditional machine learning and deep learning models, but training data scarcity is a major limitation. Overcoming this challenge, a data enhancement technique is introduced that leverages a transformer model to expand training datasets, thereby improving the performance of the deep learning-based grading system. The proposed approach utilizes a transformer model to generate and augment labels for existing unlabeled data, thereby increasing the training dataset size. The technique is successfully applied to the 2014 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) writing assessment, resulting in improved performance of the deep learning model on the testing dataset. The experiment demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves comparable performance to a fully-supervised model, thereby mitigating the negative impact of data scarcity in automated essay scoring.

In the field of multivariate statistics, focusing on extreme events is crucial.  This course aims to introduce various techniques for examining marginal dependence, which involves analyzing relationships between the most extreme occurrences in different dimensions.  We will explore methods for dimension reduction and fitting simplified models to data, as well as the development of these models from theoretical perspectives.  A key challenge lies in creating reliable methods for parameter estimation, which often involve difficult integrals.  We will demonstrate the application of these techniques using real-world data sets, which can be accessed through the book's companion website.

A research paper examines an intergenerational social model that allocates opportunities across generations. The study focuses on how opportunities are distributed and how this allocation impacts mobility between generations. The authors use mathematics to demonstrate that as the number of opportunities increases, the level of mobility tends to stabilize at a specific value. They also show that as the total number of opportunities in a society increases, the rate at which this convergence occurs also increases. Additionally, the research reveals that a specific condition must be met for the convergence rate to consistently increase with the total number of opportunities, and it is shown that this rate cannot monotonically decrease under all circumstances.

The relationship between a particle's spin and its statistical behavior is typically explained through the exchange operator $\hat{P}_{12}$, which swaps two identical particles and imparts either a $+1$ or $-1$ phase shift, resulting in symmetric or antisymmetric wave functions, respectively. However, this explanation has a fundamental issue: the exchange operator is not physically realizable as it doesn't correspond to a genuine spatial transformation. To resolve this problem, we propose an alternative explanation based on the principle of spatial symmetry, which is an inherent property of physical systems. According to this principle, any physical operation that swaps two particles can be equivalently described as a spatial transformation, ensuring that the wave function changes in a consistent manner.

We propose an upgrade to the RingCT protocol, enabling faster and more efficient anonymous transactions in Monero, by modifying the ring signature technique to take advantage of shared resources. This modification maintains the same level of security as the original RingCT, while reducing the computational load on signers, allowing for anonymous transactions of any size at a constant rate.

This study investigates the minimum memory required for solving a structured linear system on a machine with limited memory, in the RAM model. The researchers establish a lower bound for preconditioning and factorization methods, demonstrating that on a machine with n^(1+epsilon) memory, these algorithms necessitate at least n^(epsilon) memory. The lower bound applies to various matrix formulations, including banded, block-banded, triangular, and other structured matrices, as well as generalized eigenvalue problems, under the condition that epsilon is less than 0.11. The techniques employed in this work are versatile and can be applied to other problems, such as sparse matrix multiplication and the construction of a sparse inverse. The techniques are also utilized in the context of the fully-dynamic sparse matrix inverse problem.

Using data collected by the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC in 2016, an examination of top quark and W boson production processes has been conducted. This analysis involves studying events containing three massive gauge bosons, specifically focusing on the lepton-plus-multiple-jets and same-sign-dilepton-plus-multiple-jets signatures. The study utilized a total of 35.9 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity. Existing limitations on the interactions of top quarks and their possible connections to new physics have been established through measurements of various signal components.

Hebrew is one of the top ten most spoken languages globally, yet existing Hebrew NLP systems lag significantly behind state-of-the-art models for other major languages. We aim to address this disparity by leveraging a recently enhanced UD Hebrew treebank to develop improved models. Our research demonstrates that pre-trained BERT models can achieve substantial parsing accuracy, surpassing traditional unidirectional HMM-based models by a notable margin. Moreover, we find that pre-trained models exhibit remarkable robustness, successfully adapting to various cross-domain testing conditions with high parsing precision.

This paper demonstrates that most subsets of the l_p space maintain their full dimension when distorted slightly, specifically showing that in dimensions greater than or equal to 1/2, a vast majority of subsets reduce dimension by only a negligible amount under incompressible embeddings that decrease dimension.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning have led to the rapid development of data-driven modeling techniques. These models can be trained independently, yet their underlying complexities necessitate significant expertise in machine learning and theoretical foundations. This independence creates a barrier for domain experts, limiting their involvement in the model development process. To address this challenge, this paper proposes the concept of collaborative data-driven modeling, which integrates data science and domain expertise to produce more transparent and interpretable models. This paper outlines a collaborative framework and compares it to the traditional, isolated approach, highlighting the collaborative model's superior performance through case studies in two distinct domains.

We've developed a method to create LDPC codes with deleted edges in the Tanner graph.
Our approach modifies existing LDPC code creation methods to add correlations between the code's degree distribution and degree-degree correlations.
We've analyzed how these correlations impact LDPC code performance over the binary deletion channel using density evolution.
Simulation results confirm that these correlated deletion channels can improve the reliability of LDPC codes over this channel.

This research aims to develop an advanced predictive control method for linear systems that have multiple constraints. The proposed approach ensures that a system's operations remain fault-tolerant within its operational boundaries, even when disturbances occur. By formulating complex constraints in a more manageable form, we convert them into quadratic constraints. The solution involves utilizing an algorithm based on system-level synthesis to find an optimal solution to this quadratic constraint, which can be achieved through breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems. The results show that this new method significantly reduces computation time while maintaining close proximity to the best possible control outcome.

An efficient quantum key distribution system relies on the decoy state method to prevent eavesdroppers from gaining excessive information about the key. Although calculating the optimal key allocation probability for this method is complicated, approximations based on small error probabilities have been the standard approach. In this study, we present a novel key allocation probability that linearly reduces with error probability, marking an improvement over previous methods. Furthermore, we explore how this probability affects the system's secret key rate and compare it with other schemes. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed probability not only limits the eavesdropper's information gain but also minimizes the key allocation probability, thereby enhancing the system's efficiency and making it more resilient to attacks.

Recent breakthroughs in large-scale language models have significantly advanced the field of natural language processing. This paper delves into the pretraining influence on in-context learning capabilities of a 175-billion-parameter model, specifically examining the role of pretraining corpora. By utilizing the 175-billion-parameter model, we investigate how in-context learning is affected by varying pretraining corpora, and our results show that the model's language understanding and generation capabilities can be significantly enhanced through the incorporation of high-quality, domain-specific data. This study sheds new light on the pretraining process and its long-term implications for the development of advanced NLP models.

To understand the process of galaxy cluster cores breaking out of thermal equilibrium, we employed a two-dimensional numerical simulation that incorporates the effects of cooling, cooling-breaks, and cooling-runaway. In our model, three-dimensional turbulence is represented by an energy injection mechanism, and the interaction between cooling and turbulent heating is studied. Our results show that in low-metallicity environments, thermal instability can be suppressed, and the development of cold clouds is inhibited. However, in environments with higher metallicities, cold clouds can grow and fragment, and the effects of radiative cooling are amplified. In these scenarios, the growth of cold clouds is found to be independent of the initial temperature and is facilitated by the convergence of hot and cold gas. Our model also reveals that magnetic field effects and thermal conduction can influence the development of thermal instability, and the results are discussed in the context of galaxy cluster observations.

The interplay between CPT symmetry and the S matrix in the Standard Model can be understood through the concept of CP violation in Weyl spinors, which serves as the fundamental source. The CPT theorem can be redefined as a theorem on quantum operators, providing a new perspective. The classification of CP violation based on beauty and elegance provides insights into different types of violation, including explicit, spontaneous, and anomalous forms. The notion of elegance in this context refers to the minimum number of Weyl spinors required to express the CPT-violating term in the effective Lagrangian. We demonstrate that CPT even four-fermion interactions exhibiting CP violation require at least eight Weyl spinors, while certain CP-violating three-fermion interactions can be described using just two spinors, including a specific interaction between a neutrino, a positron, and a neutral pion.

In the context of superstring theory, we've analyzed hard scattering processes and found that the coefficients of the leading Regge trajectory, specifically at powers of $s/M_{st}^2$, are rational multiples of $\pi$ and involve the coefficients of a specific elliptic curve. These results confirm a previous hypothesis proposed by Gross, which stated that such $\pi$-dependent coefficients are universal across all superstring theories, independent of the specific model. Furthermore, we've discovered that the coefficients of higher-order terms in the expansion are not necessarily rational, challenging the broader applicability of Gross's hypothesis.

As 5G networks approach deployment, their vast scale and complexity pose significant management challenges. To mitigate these issues, the concept of self-organizing networks (SON) has emerged, aiming to automate network configuration and optimization. This paper outlines the core administrative procedures used to manage a 5G cellular network, including processes for handling configuration updates, performance monitoring, and policy adjustments. By integrating SON technologies, the goal is to achieve optimal network efficiency and sustainability with minimal manual intervention.

In the field of speech synthesis, recent breakthroughs in end-to-end models have led to innovative approaches for generating high-quality speech. Building on this progress, we introduce a novel technique for resource-constrained speech synthesis, utilizing a dictionary of acoustic units to represent universal phonemes. This technique involves creating a compact model using permutation invariant neural networks and a unit-level representation, allowing it to distinguish between units with the same phoneme. This model is then used to synthesize speech by combining the most suitable acoustic units. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in the TIMIT evaluation and achieve a significant improvement in speech quality compared to a baseline model using a traditional HMM.

Convex optimization is a widely used technique for solving motion planning problems due to its efficiency and reliability. However, the practical application of convex optimization often suffers from subpar solutions, primarily attributed to overly restrictive assumptions made during problem formulation. To address this challenge, this paper presents an innovative two-step process for improving motion planning problems involving complex constraints and coupled convex optimization problems. Initially, parameters for a simplified model of the problem are learned from data, allowing for tighter constraints and more feasible solutions. Subsequently, these refined parameters are applied to significantly improve the quality of solutions obtained. Experimental results demonstrate a substantial reduction in constraint violations and a considerable decrease in computational time, particularly for coupled convex optimization problems.

We investigate the concept of converting one quantum state to another using randomised procedures limited by a specific number of copies of the states involved, with conversion confirmed when a specific detection sequence occurs. Our findings demonstrate that this testing protocol is effective in assessing the convertibility of quantum states within a specific class, including states belonging to the multiprobing class, with the number of required detections scaling logarithmically with the system dimension. Our experiments, implemented on superconducting circuits, confirm the effectiveness of this testing protocol and reveal instances where the limited use of copies hinders reliable characterization of quantum states.

The movement of a fluid within a container on a rotating base can be likened to the behavior of two masses connected by a spring, where the base's motion is the driving force. The connection between the base and the fluid is characterized by a combination of frictional and pressure forces. The amount of fluid within the container has a significant impact on the nature of the fluid's response to the base's motion, particularly when the motion is periodic. When the container is only partially filled, the fluid's movement is typically irregular and unpredictable. However, when the container is nearly full, the fluid's movement is usually periodic and in sync with the base's motion, the ratio of the in-phase component to the out-of-phase component increasing with the ratio of the driving force to the damping force, the fluid's response exhibiting characteristics of a low-Q mechanical system, the fluid moving in an elliptical pattern, the in-phase component dominating when the damping is low, and both components being in phase when the damping is very high.

In the field of machine learning, distributed training is a common technique used in large-scale data center environments. However, when devices are deployed in distributed settings, the risk of data privacy breaches increases due to centralized algorithms' vulnerabilities. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a robust method for training machine learning models across a network of connected devices, taking into account the irregular structure of the communication network and potential divergence from expected data distributions. This approach combines elements of decentralized learning and risk minimization under uncertainty, resulting in improved model performance compared to existing methods. We evaluate the performance of our method on real-world data sets and demonstrate its effectiveness in producing more accurate models.

We investigate the initial conditions of nuclear collisions and the process of hydrodynamization, focusing on both single-nucleon collisions and high-energy nuclear collisions. 
In the context of single-nucleon collisions, along the longitudinal direction, energy is transferred in the form of soft gluons, leading to an anisotropic state. 
By applying a truncated expansion of the Boltzmann equation, we examine how this evolution develops and compare it to relativistic fluid dynamics. 
Our results show that hydrodynamic behavior emerges rapidly, within a few units of the medium's density, allowing for the creation of relativistic particles even in infrequent nuclear collisions. 
Furthermore, we analyze the energy distribution and the characteristics of these early-stage conditions, obtaining novel insights into the formation of quark-gluon plasma in relativistic nuclear collisions.

The velocity distribution of low-velocity outflows from star-forming regions is not uniform, and the mechanisms behind this variability are still unclear. The velocity pattern of high-velocity jets is also not well-understood, and the factors contributing to this velocity pattern are still not fully understood. The relationship between jet velocity and the velocity distribution of low-velocity outflows is still not well-established. To gain a better understanding of this, we conducted a study of 13 star-forming regions using the ALMA telescope, and the results showed that the velocity distribution of molecular jets is not well-defined and the velocities of these jets are not consistently correlated with the mass of the protostar. The study also showed that the angular momentum of the protostars is not well-defined and the angular momentum distribution is not consistently correlated with the mass of the protostar. The results suggest that the variability in the angular momentum of the protostars may be the key factor contributing to the variability in the velocity distribution of low-velocity outflows. The study suggests that the angular momentum of the protostars may be the key factor contributing to the variability in the velocity distribution of low-velocity outflows.

This study focuses on developing a performance-safety balance approach for nonlinear systems subject to limitations. The proposed method involves two complementary strategies: a safety filter that ensures feasibility and boundedness of the system's trajectory, and an equilibrated control framework that optimizes performance while maintaining safety. By integrating these approaches, the equilibrated bounded performance-safety (EBAP) problem is effectively addressed, and the concept of the safety margin is utilized to enhance performance. The proposed strategy is validated through simulation of a constrained mobile robot navigating a maze.

This research paper conducts a comprehensive analytical and numerical investigation into the dynamics of Solar Radiation Pressure (SRP) for orbits in solar system bodies' Hill-Czsarny regions. The analysis begins with an in-depth examination of SRP models and their impact on orbit types under the influence of SRP, specifically focusing on semi-secular resonances that arise due to SRP perturbations. The study then evaluates various analytical and numerical methods for detecting these resonances and their boundaries, comparing the effectiveness of different approaches such as the Analytical Model, Monte-Carlo simulations, and machine learning algorithms. The research considers two distinct scenarios: one involving orbits around the Earth and the other around a smaller celestial body in 1:1 resonance, each with unique SRP characteristics. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of SRP orbit dynamics and the potential applications of these findings in orbit design and management.

The behavior of light interacting with matter is accurately simulated using a first-principle tight-binding model that ensures both spatial and temporal homogeneity. The model's mathematical formulation guarantees invariance under translations of space and time, which is further validated by its four-operator structure. The underlying physics is further confirmed by the relationship between the electric field and the time derivative of the vector potential, resulting in a final form that is invariant under a gauge transformation that is both spatially and temporally homogeneous.

This research focuses on solving the object perception task by leveraging both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints as input data. A specific category-specific form is assumed for each object, and our proposed method involves learning a compact, compacted 3D form representation for each object category from unaligned training data. A novel cost function is introduced to measure the discrepancy between observed data and predicted form, and an optimization technique is used to identify the most probable Form-Associated Pose (FAP) for the object given the available data. Furthermore, a novel cost function is proposed to evaluate the difference between the observed keypoint data and the predicted FAP, and the optimal pose that minimizes this difference is identified. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our method in both 2D and 3D object pose estimation tasks.

This project aims to address the specific problem of determining the confidence interval for a Cauchy distribution, taking into account the distribution's characteristic parameter of location. To achieve this goal, the concept of the highest density region is utilized, and the expectation–maximization algorithm is employed to estimate the Cauchy parameters based on observed data. Furthermore, the location of the maximum expectation probability, in relation to the cauchy parameters, is investigated, and the feasibility of applying Newton's method in this context is considered.

A type of clinical trial known as the basket trial is conducted by testing an intervention across multiple distinct patient groups in parallel.  By allowing data from different arms to inform one another, researchers can potentially reduce the overall trial size and increase statistical power.  Bayesian methods using predictive probability have been developed to determine an appropriate sample size for each arm while accounting for information borrowing.  This study aims to evaluate various approaches for posterior predictive sample size determination in trials with multiple groups and subsets that share data.  Through the use of simulation, researchers compared different formulas based on their performance in terms of actual and estimated sample sizes.  The results show that one specific method outperforms other existing approaches and provides R code for implementing this methodology.

Achieving high precision in motion control systems can be effectively managed using control theory, specifically through the application of Linear Parameter Varying (LPV) controllers in conjunction with supply function augmentation. Although this method yields significant results, it is often overly complex and computationally intensive. To streamline this process, we can simplify the synthesis of an LPV controller by employing a sequential approach. By utilizing supply function augmentation within each step of this sequential procedure, high-performance motion control systems can be developed more efficiently. To illustrate the feasibility of this simplified strategy, a practical case study involving a piezo actuator will be examined.

Deep learning models, particularly those used in medical imaging, heavily rely on fully paired data for effective 3D registration, but such data is often costly and difficult to obtain in a labeled format. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the concept of partial-to-partial alignment in the context of 3D point clouds, addressing scenarios where complete data points are not available for certain applications like incomplete medical scans. To tackle this complex challenge, we propose a novel Relational Network for Efficient Transfer (PRNet), which learns to align incomplete 3D point clouds in a self-supervised manner. By leveraging efficient nearest-neighbor searches and a novel graph-based data representation, PRNet can effectively capture the geometric properties of point clouds and facilitate their alignment. Our approach is notably simpler and more scalable than existing methods, achieving superior performance across various benchmark datasets for both our proposed task and complete-to-complete alignment.

The R_infinity property, which describes an infinite number of conjugacy classes that are torsion-based, is being examined in relation to certain groups, specifically generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups and their nested structures, including the upper central series. We have found that certain groups possess the R_infinity property, while others do not, and our findings are not uniform across all nilpotent groups, showing that the R_infinity property is not necessarily inherited by all nilpotent quotients.

Current measurements of Standard Model parameters are consistent with the model's vacuum being in a metastable state, likely due to the mass of the top quark, and the likelihood of this situation becoming more pronounced over time. To further investigate the degree of metastability and determine its implications for the universe's future, more precise measurements of these parameters are necessary. This can be achieved by obtaining top quark pair samples at high luminosities at either the High-Luminosity LHC or a future circular collider, and by measuring the Higgs boson mass at an electron-positron collider, such as the Circular Electron Positron Collider or the Future Circular Collider in electron mode.

In time-resolved data analysis, a method is developed using the ultrafast electron diffraction technique to model atomic movements. A key challenge in analyzing this type of data is the unreliable nature of weak signals due to noise, which often leads to overfitting models. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that incorporates constraints into the model optimization process. The constraints are set up using electron diffraction patterns and enforced during the optimization of the model. The proposed approach is tested on both simulated and real data from LaAlO3, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing robust atomic trajectories that are not overly influenced by noise.
The study calculates and compares the distribution profiles of the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons, with a focus on their radial excitations.

We derive direct Fourier-based criteria for the membership of elements in the Gelfand-Shilov spaces and prove that certain weighted composition operators on specific spaces are non-trivial. The findings have implications for the nature of Toeplitz operators when applied to certain function spaces.

Segmentation tasks across different imaging modalities often require extensive, costly manual annotation due to severe domain shift. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that leverages cycle-consistent adversarial networks to split different modalities without labeled data. Our method not only addresses domain shift but also enhances cycle-consistent image segmentation by producing sharper boundaries. Thorough experiments on the Synapse dataset, involving comparisons with cutting-edge techniques and ablation studies, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in handling multimolaI segmentation challenges with domain shift.

Although Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) excel at sequence modeling, they often struggle with long-term dependencies and can be inefficient due to their fixed time steps. To overcome these limitations, this paper presents an alternative approach that utilizes Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernelized RNNs. By integrating the RBF kernel into the RNN architecture, this method effectively handles long-term dependencies and enables the modeling of actions at variable time steps. The proposed action prediction framework, based on the RBF-KFM RNN, demonstrates superior performance on two benchmark datasets when compared to state-of-the-art methods.

A remarkable solar flare occurred on April 12, 1985, from the star AD Leo, 
characterized by significant X-ray and UV emissions. This study simulates the 
continuum radiation produced by the flare, focusing on electron interactions with 
the star's atmosphere and the resulting UV emissions between 200 and 300 nm. 
The simulations utilize a two-component flare model, incorporating nonthermal 
electron impacts and energy distribution. By comparing the model's predictions with 
actual observations, researchers find that the model's continuum radiation is 
consistent with observed data, particularly in the 200-250 nm range. However, 
discrepancies arise in the 250-300 nm range, where the model underestimates the 
observed radiation. This discrepancy may be attributed to factors such as 
energy-dependent electron interactions or additional heating mechanisms.

We are examining the deformation theory of G2-instantons within the context of nearly G2 geometries. A key finding reveals that the space of infinitesimal deformations of an oriented triaxial ellipsoid Hopf G2-instantant on a nearly G2 six-manifold is equivalent to the space of antisymmetric 2-forms. Furthermore, the map defining the complex for these deformations demonstrates that this space is isomorphic to the cohomology group of 2-forms with zero divergence. The study concludes with a demonstration that, in general, this deformation theory exhibits non-linearity.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a finite dimension is regarded as $C$-normal if it satisfies the equation $C^{*}TC=C T C^{*}$. The condition for the weighted composition operator $C_{\phi,B}$ to be $C$-normal on the Hardy space $H^2$ has been examined, where it is defined by $(C_{\phi,B}f)(z)=f(\phi(z))B(z)$, with the operator $B$ being an analytic function on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ and $\phi$ being an analytic function on the $\mathbb{D}$ with the derivative at zero not equal to zero.

We investigated the count of large p-core p'-partitions with n parts, which correspond to specific walks on a graph representing addition modulo p, starting from a specified node and covering exactly n edges. These partitions were previously linked to the work of Andrews on parts with limited differences, and our contribution extends this area by examining the total number of such partitions across all possible part sizes.

Three-dimensional object modeling is a fundamental task in computer vision, but existing methods often overlook the issue of topology ambiguity in point cloud models. A single image can only convey limited spatial information, and the model topology can vary significantly even when generated from the same image through different transformations. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that combines a 3D denoiser and topology predictor using a feedback loop. The proposed method transforms point cloud models into a canonical form to facilitate accurate topology prediction and utilizes predicted topological errors to refine noisy point clouds obtained through 3D denoising. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing high-quality, error-free 3D models that are consistent across different transformations.

In a network of Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) sensors, multiple signals can overlap, leading to interference and inaccurate time measurements. To address this issue, two methods for mitigating interference are examined: one using slotting techniques and another employing channel assignment. The effectiveness of these approaches is evaluated through simulation, with a focus on improving measurement precision and reducing interference effects.

This study examines how Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is affected by entwin two-photon absorption (ETPA) in superconducting Josephson junction single-photon detectors. The ETPA process can interfere with spectral measurements, so researchers investigated its implications for spectral evaluations of quantum light sources. The study found that Hahn echo measurements, which are used to assess spectral properties, are immune to ETPA interference, but other measurement methods, such as standard QND, may be affected. The study indicates that adjusting how photons are applied can mitigate ETPA's impact, offering a potential solution for spectral evaluations.

We establish that elliptic cohomology exhibits $T$-equivariance in relation to $\mathbb{C}P(V)$, with $\mathbb{C}^*$ acting on it, by creating the endofunctor $E_X(-)\otimes E_{\mathbb{C}P(V)}(X)$, which is equivalent to $E_X(-)\otimes_{E_{\mathbb{C}^*}} E_{\mathbb{C}^*}(\mathbb{C}P(V))$, and proving it has a well-defined structure as a comonadic object within the category of $T$-equivariant $E_X(X)$-bimodules.

Temporal knowledge graph completion involves predicting missing facts in dynamic datasets by leveraging temporal information.
Current models typically assume a specific representation for each entity, relation, and temporal feature.
In this work, we propose assuming a linear representation for entities, relations, and temporal features instead.
This assumption enables sharing representation parameters across multiple entities, relations, or temporal features, which is beneficial in scenarios with numerous entities, relations, or temporal features but few facts.
We also assume low-rank matrices for these representation parameters, which further promotes parameter sharing and enhances model generalization.
This paper's contributions include: (1) formulating assumptions for linear and low-rank representations in knowledge graph completion, (2) developing an efficient optimization algorithm based on alternating minimization and block coordinate descent, and (3) conducting comprehensive experiments on KG24 dataset showing the superiority of our models.

In the Gielgud production of Hamlet, a 1950s sound effect known as "ground sound" was introduced by sound designer John B. Williams. This technique, characterized by low rumbling noises, has been the subject of debate among scholars regarding its purpose and impact. This research investigates "ground sound" by examining its acoustic properties and exploring how it influences audience perception of space and perspective. By analyzing its occurrence in the play and considering historical context, the study ultimately proposes that "ground sound" functions as a narrative device to convey character-driven "poetic logic" to the audience.

In quantum physics, demonstrating Bell nonlocality without inequalities has been a significant goal.  A specific scenario has been identified where nonlocal correlations can be definitively proven using a single measurement from each of the sender and receiver, even when these correlations are not in an ideal state.  This demonstration is possible because of the unique correlation properties that arise when sending two perfectly correlated bits over a quantum channel, which are not possible with a single bit.  As a result, nonlocal correlations can be definitively proven using these unique properties, offering new opportunities for practical applications.

This study revisits fundamental concepts of flat lines, their inherent properties, and the techniques for their identification and generation within the context of electron transport measurements. We examine the relationship between these measurements and a material's electronic band structure, emphasizing the significance of both theoretical and experimental approaches in understanding flat lines. We illustrate the practical applications of flat bands in physics, particularly in understanding unconventional magnetic behaviors and highly correlated electrical properties. Furthermore, this work showcases the novel potential of flat bands in the development of topologically protected devices and highly efficient, low-power electronic components.

Recent experiments have demonstrated superconductivity in certain materials like boron sulfide and selenium at relatively low temperatures and moderate pressure levels. Theoretical predictions suggest that certain hydrogen-boron compounds could exhibit even higher superconducting critical temperatures in the same pressure range. We have investigated the electronic properties of two such materials, monolayer hydrogen borosulfide and bilayer hydrogen boroselenide, using first-principles calculations. The results indicate that these materials exhibit some degree of superconductivity, with the electron-phonon coupling being stronger in monolayer hydrogen borosulfide. The superconducting critical temperatures were predicted to be around 10 K and 12 K, with the latter exceeding the former. The electron mobility was found to be higher in monolayer hydrogen borosulfide compared to boron arsenide. The superconducting properties of these materials are attributed to their van der Waals forces, which allow for high carrier mobility and sufficient phonon softness.

The allocation of CPU time to processes is a fundamental aspect of operating systems, with various strategies employed to achieve this, including partitioning methods. Although some processes may utilize more CPU time than others, traditional partitioning methods often result in inefficient resource usage. In this research, a new approach based on an adapted version of the Flattened Partitioning method is proposed, combining an algorithm inspired by the Knapsack problem to maximize the utilization of CPU time per process, while maintaining each process within its allocated time limit. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing solutions, particularly in terms of reducing the waiting time for processes, with experiments conducted on simulated workloads validating its effectiveness.

In this study, we delve into the low-temperature state of charm hadron matter, 
incorporating both static and dynamic quarks within the framework of 2+1 flavor 
dynamic lattice QCD, in accordance with the latest lattice configurations from the 
Physically-Quenched (PQ) and Physical settings. By analyzing the temperature 
dependence of the speed of sound, we establish the presence of a phase transition, 
characterized by a sudden stiffening of the speed of sound, mirroring the behavior 
observed in the absence of strange quarks. Furthermore, we investigate the impact 
of finite strange quark mass on this transition, discovering that the transition 
strength diminishes as the strange quark mass increases, ultimately leading to a 
smooth transition in the four-flavor scenario. This work contributes to a deeper 
understanding of the equation of state governing the quark-gluon plasma state.

Automotive systems with fail-operational capabilities play a vital role in the widespread adoption of highly automated driving systems. The robust performance of these systems can be enhanced by integrating redundant safety checks that kick in when primary systems malfunction. A formal verification process for such automotive systems, which incorporate fail-operational mechanisms, redundancy management, and safety protocol deactivation, has been developed using the model checker UPPAAL. The approach involves the creation of a system model that accounts for complex decision-making processes and is then validated against a set of temporal properties that ensure safe operation. The validation process, applied to a fail-operational hailing system, demonstrates the efficacy of the verification method in confirming safe system performance.

A dynamic system's state can be divided into distinct categories based on its future behavior, which is crucial in various fields, including forecasting the movement of balls in a pinball machine or assessing the impact of disturbances on power grids. Systems exhibiting similar responses to disturbances are often grouped together, but the effectiveness of these clusters in representing safe areas may vary. We propose a method to identify dynamic systems that react consistently to disturbances, which can be applied to both observable and non-observable systems. Our approach utilizes an optimized measure of the difference between trajectories, which is then used to develop a solution for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, allowing us to assess the system's response to disturbances. We demonstrate the applicability of this method through the analysis of numerical examples, including a double integrator, a pendulum, and a simulated aircraft.

Infinitesimal calculus has been the subject of controversy due to its unclear foundational logic. Historically, Leibniz's calculus relied on the notion of infinitesimals, but this concept has long been considered problematic. Despite this, the practical application of infinitesimals has remained unchanged, and modern mathematical frameworks have successfully reintroduced the concept in three distinct ways. This account aims to highlight the key features of these frameworks - Non-Standard Analysis, Infinitesimal Analysis, and Ideal Analysis - and their historical connections to Leibniz's original reasoning.

The use of interferometry for intensity mapping with 21 cm signals from Hydrogen is a promising technique for studying the era of cosmic dawn and retreating darkness.  However, removing galactic interference from foreground signals is a significant challenge.  Recent research has developed an algorithm to eliminate real-time foreground noise through a model-based approach.  This study examines how the foreground removal process affects power spectra and confidence intervals under various scenarios.  Our findings indicate that removing the interference can distort the phase spectrum and affect the reliability of cosmological parameters.  To mitigate these effects, we suggest employing robust foreground removal methods and using larger telescopes with better sensitivity and higher angular resolution.

Independence is a fundamental concept in both quantum information theory and stochastic processes, with its mathematical underpinnings still being clarified. By combining rigorous mathematical analysis and intuitive physical examples, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of independence. In particular, we focus on the Fock space representation, which offers a practical and easily applicable framework for working with independence. This approach is particularly useful in quantum information theory, where its simplicity and effectiveness are highlighted.

Recommender systems are essential in bridging the gap between an abundance of online information and the time-constrained nature of modern society. Despite the proliferation of various recommender system types, such as content-based and collaborative filtering, each has its own shortcomings. Content-based methods struggle with the diversity of user preferences, while collaborative filtering systems face the challenges of the cold-start and similarity issues. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored the potential of hybrid methods that combine different approaches. This paper proposes an enhanced hybrid recommender system that integrates both context-based document ranking and user behavior-based methods. By leveraging advanced NLP techniques, the proposed system can accurately predict and display the most relevant documents for a given user query, taking into account their individual interests and browsing patterns.

We investigate the openness of free probability phenomena, particularly type $B$ openness and matrix multiplicative deformations, in the context of random matrix theory. Our approach involves analyzing the typical behavior of large random matrices with independent entries. We demonstrate that certain polynomial functions of these matrices retain independence under small deformations, regardless of the underlying probability distribution of the entries, as long as certain conditions are met. This leads to the conclusion that free random matrices exhibit a level of stability, or "openness," in their deformed counterparts. As a result, we obtain explicit calculations for the free additive and multiplicative convolution operations.

This study introduces a LINDIGEN-style model checker for timed properties, which is a more intuitive alternative to traditional linear temporal logic (LTL) by allowing property specification in terms of events occurring at specific times. The specification language, timed event structure logic (TESL), retains the expressive capabilities of LTL while significantly simplifying the process of creating meaningful properties. The underlying algorithm for timed model checking has been adapted from a liveness-checking procedure developed for two systems, resulting in a method that incorporates two distinct processes: one for checking the fit of system traces with an simplified, prioritized version of the TESL property, and another for identifying any model trace that fails to satisfy the property. The revised algorithm has been implemented in a new model checker, which has been thoroughly tested against various existing and newly discovered potential issues in system behavior, many of which were previously analyzed in existing research.

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ is investigated in an unconventional framework where the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ scalar resonances merge into a single continuum. A formula is developed to describe the line shape of the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ interference in terms of the $\pi^0 \eta$ two-body scattering amplitude. Calculations utilizing this approach align well with experimental findings from CDF, LHCb, Belle, and BaBar.

The GRAVITY gathering camera is a crucial addition to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, allowing it to combine light from different telescope mirrors. This unique capability enables the GRAVITY observing mode, which has become the most frequently used on the VLT in recent years. The device consists of a sophisticated setup that light passes through before reaching the detector, and although the detector is shared with the VLT, it can be reconfigured for other applications. The GRAVITY observing mode offers exceptional performance with picometer-level precision in position and flux measurements. The device's unique properties have enabled groundbreaking research in various fields, including the study of stellar surfaces, the behavior of active galactic nuclei, and the surface movements of T Tauri stars.

The objective of the k-center problem with arbitrary cost functions is to select k points from a given set X, in order to minimize the maximum distance between any point in X and its nearest selected point. In the specific case where the metric space has a constant doubling dimension, we demonstrate how to find a constant-factor approximation for the k-center problem. Conversely, we establish that achieving a certain level of accuracy beyond a certain threshold would require exponential time, assuming the uniqueness of a widely accepted hypothesis.

In this paper, F. Grossmann's concept of the shift operator is utilized to define the notion of entire functions with the displacement property, and the identities J=I and J=I^-1 are introduced to represent the invariance of these functions under the displacement operation. The order of such functions is denoted by ρ, and it is assumed that they are linearly independent from the exponential polynomial P(z), which occurs at least finitely often. Specifically, the current investigation focuses on the circumstances under which both P(z) and its derivative P'(z) share the same finite set E of critical points, and it is demonstrated that under the given assumptions, P(z) is indeed an entire function.

In 1990, Fitchtingh and Schoenmakers introduced an algorithm for solving linear systems over polynomial rings, incorporating random error to handle systems with multiple solutions. This was later enhanced by Kalkbrener in 1997, who developed a more robust algorithm with earlier termination capabilities. Our study provides a simplified algorithm with comparable performance guarantees, along with an improved bound on computational complexity. Specifically, we show that for a ring with n variables and a Groebner basis with d terms, each having a maximum coefficient size of δ and vector length of l, the algorithm requires at most O((n+l)δ^2d^4) arithmetic operations in a basic computational ring.

The parity of photons is difficult to define and measure due to the constraints of free space, but researchers have found a way to define and individually control the parity of photons using nanoscale cavities with protected parity states. The parity of photons can be individually detected with high efficiency using superconducting phase qubits coupled to the cavities. Furthermore, the researchers have demonstrated the first generation of photonic quantum states protected by symmetry, achieving this through the purification of mixed states without measuring the photons. The discovery paves the way for developing parity-protected quantum communication networks, where quantum information can be transmitted and processed with enhanced stability and reliability.

We have developed an accurate analytical model for the equilibrium state of a single-component plasma made up of alkali atoms. The pressure of this plasma is divided into two components: the ideal gas pressure and the pressure resulting from interactions between particles. The model is based on a Fourier series expansion of the potential energy of the plasma, which is derived from Monte Carlo simulations. The single-particle density of the plasma is also calculated using this model. The model is then applied to the case of cesium and its thermodynamic properties are compared with existing models. The model is found to be in good agreement with molecular dynamics simulations and is simpler than previous models.

In the vector meson spectrum, we have calculated the spectral function, taking into account the influence of chiral asymmetry on vector mesons, as represented by the fermion vacuum. The relevant interaction is described by the Lagrangian, and the self-energy of vector mesons is determined through a diagrammatic approach. The results show that the mass of the vector mesons is affected by chiral asymmetry, with the impact varying based on the meson's quantum numbers. The interaction with the medium leads to the broadening of the vector mesons' spectral function.

This research introduces and evaluates the concept of network scale, defined as the ratio of average path length to diameter in a network. The proposed definition is then applied to design and analyze an algorithm for estimating a small-world network's scale under the assumption of at most f faulty nodes. We present both a lower bound on this scale and an algorithm that can accurately estimate it within a constant factor under the assumption of a sufficiently large diameter relative to f. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the network is generated according to a specific GNP model with a parameter that results in a small, O(f) diameter, no estimation method can achieve even additive accuracy under the assumption of a sufficiently large f relative to log n.

In numerical relativity simulations, the initial data constraints are typically addressed by employing the conformal transverse-traceless decomposition. The new method CTTK directly solves these constraints using a single system of partial differential equations. CTTK is being integrated into the SpEC code to explore its benefits and potential applications, including its possible use as a more efficient alternative in specific scenarios where diagonal systems are advantageous.

The JUNO experiment, a large-scale water-Cherenkov detector with 20,000 tons of target material, will utilize 12,600 30-inch PMTs to precisely measure neutrino oscillation parameters $\sin^2\theta_{12}$ and $\sin^2\theta_{13}$ over a wide energy range. Accurate knowledge of the PMT mass collection efficiency is crucial for achieving the experiment's goals. Our study involves detailed analysis of 20-inch PMTs used in JUNO, including mass collection efficiency measurements and gain stability assessments. We also examine the electric field distribution within the detector and its potential impact on efficiency. Our findings indicate that the average mass collection efficiency for 20-inch PMTs is 0.995 with a standard deviation of 0.001, and the PMTs maintain consistent performance over time with minimal fluctuations.

The performance of multivariate time series forecasting can be significantly improved by leveraging the interconnections between related variables. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) can model these variable relationships by using a graph structure that defines relationships between nodes representing time series. However, the graph structure used in GCNs for time series prediction is typically either randomly generated or based on the user's understanding of the data, which can lead to suboptimal results. To address this limitation, a novel method called AGCNN has been developed that automatically generates a graph structure suitable for a given dataset. By modeling node features as a mixture of multivariate Gaussian distributions and learning the parameters, AGCNN can identify the most probable graph structure, resulting in improved prediction accuracy compared to existing GCN variants.

A precise analysis of atmospheric dispersion requires an accurate mathematical model that describes the phenomenon. In a previous study, a new model for atmospheric dispersion was developed and its predictions were compared with on-sky measurements. This comparison revealed discrepancies between the model's predictions and measured values. The current study aims to address these differences by examining the assumptions underlying the model. By relaxing these constraints, we found that increasing the air pressure near the ground and incorporating a temperature inversion near the ground can resolve the model's issues. However, these adjustments introduce new challenges, such as the air pressure exceeding that at sea level and the need to refine the model's treatment of atmospheric density fluctuations.

We introduce a novel approach to training models with multiple instructors by developing the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) algorithm, which combines several expert opinions through an iterative process. Our method outperforms using a single instructor and also surpasses established multi-instructor techniques on a range of tasks, including binary classification and multi-label classification. The advantages of the method stem from its ability to leverage pairwise comparisons, which are more effective than direct predictions in reconciling conflicting expert opinions. The name PILE reflects the two core principles underlying our approach: the use of pairwise learning and iterative model refinement.

We suggest a novel approach to detect shadow matter using a network of geographically dispersed sensors. This approach, based on intensity interferometry, a technique originally employed in astronomy, involves analyzing sensor output data to measure correlations in signal fluctuations. These correlations can be used to pinpoint the direction of incoming waves, specifically those generated by ultralight bosonic particles known as shadow particles, which have masses ranging from 10^-22 to 10^-19 eV. This new detection method offers a more sensitive and cost-effective means of exploring this particular range of particle masses, particularly when compared to existing atomic detectors, by exploiting a phenomenon known as Landau-Zener transitions.

This study explores B-pursuit solutions to the problem of recovering a vector x in R^n from y = Ax subject to the l_1-norm constraint, where A is a matrix with n rows and n^2 columns. We establish that for large n values, the probability of having a unique solution approaches one. This probability can be approximated using a Gaussian process, and n is estimated to be between (1/4 to 3/4) times sqrt d, with d representing the effective dimension, which is defined as the number of degrees of freedom for linear functions that map the unit l_1-norm in R^m to a set bounded by a constant C.

The P4 programmable switch architecture has become the leading choice for creating custom network applications, yet the absence of open-source P4 compilers hinders the development of innovative designs. Specifically, existing commercial compilers lack open-source support, which limits the verification and improvement opportunities for new, innovative P4 designs. To address this issue, we present P4cc, an open-source P4 compiler with a P416 architecture backend, enabling innovative designs to be tested and validated more easily. Our compiler's capabilities are demonstrated through comprehensive testing and by successfully compiling and optimizing complex P416 programs.

In the context of the discrete Hodge decomposition, solving a time-dependent vector transport equation arises frequently. However, implementing this transport equation accurately poses a challenge. This work focuses on refining numerical solutions by addressing a specific issue that occurs when the equation is discretized using certain low-order Raviart-Thomas finite elements. Although this discretization preserves the maximum norm property, it results in spurious oscillations in the computed solutions. To address this problem, we first analyze the reasons behind these inaccuracies and then propose modifications to the standard numerical method. These proposed corrections maintain the maximum norm property, thereby preventing the emergence of unrealistic oscillations. Our approach is demonstrated using a specific two-dimensional r4 mesh, and its effectiveness is confirmed by the convergence of its associated errors.

The emerging federated learning paradigm holds great promise for developing equitable and privacy-preserving AI systems. In response, we present an innovative framework for teaching fairness to local data sources within the FL network, alongside a new method for centralizing all data to ensure consistent fairness. At the same time, we introduce a decentralized differential privacy approach, combining local fairness constraints with centralized differential privacy. Our experiments demonstrate the feasibility of achieving fairness and privacy in the FL setting.

Using the LHCb experiment data collected in 2016, we found evidence for a newly discovered excited state of the $B_c^+$ particle, which decays through a chi-c intermediate state, ultimately breaking down into a $J/\psi$ and a $D^+$. The discovered state has a significance level of around 3.4 standard deviations, with a relative detection frequency of approximately 11.5 parts per million. Furthermore, our analysis did not find support for the predicted fourth excited $B_c$ state in the $D^* J/\psi$ channel, which was expected to have a relative detection frequency of around 13 parts per million.

A new numerical approach has been developed for solving the autonomous equation dy/dt = f(y), particularly considering the structure-preserving methods known as continuous-runge-kutta schemes. When the function f is both Lipschitz continuous and monotone, it has been proven that the proposed method converges with a specific order of accuracy. This proof relies on a newly discovered estimate for the trajectory of the equation, which bounds the norm of the solution y. This estimate is also applicable in solving nonlinear equations and was previously discovered in the context of Runge-Kutta methods for such problems.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have seen significant advancements in performance, 
but the complexity of large-scale DNNs poses challenges in memory and 
computational requirements. To overcome these obstacles, techniques such as 
gradient checkpointing and 32-bit precision gradients have been employed to 
enable the training of DNNs that exceed hardware memory capacity. However, 
these approaches often result in slow convergence and high communication 
overhead. In this research, we introduce the regional critic (RC) method, which 
enables model-parallel training of DNNs by splitting the model into multiple 
regions and checking for consistency across these regions. The RC method 
leverages all available device memory for the DNN parameters, reduces the 
checkpointing and gradient volume, and minimizes communication overhead. 
Compared to existing methods, the regional critic approach yields a 2.4 times
